title: Judges 16:1–3
context: Samson goes to Gaza, a major Philistine city, and spends the night with a prostitute. The Gazites wait in ambush at the city gate, but Samson rises at midnight, tears the gate out, posts and bar together, and carries it to a hill facing Hebron. The short episode sets the pattern for the Delilah story that follows: great strength joined to moral weakness, and a judge who walks into danger through his own desires.

verses.text: Samson went to Gaza, and saw there a prostitute, and went in to her.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator states the sin plainly: Samson goes in to a prostitute in an enemy city. Arminian readers see a consecrated man's real moral failure and note that his gifts did not make him immune to temptation or excuse it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise call this what it is, sin, and note that Scripture does not hide the failings of those God uses. The pattern of Samson's desires leading him into danger prepares for his fall with Delilah.

verses.text: The Gazites were told, “Samson is here!” They surrounded him and laid wait for him all night in the gate of the city, and were quiet all the night, saying, “Wait until morning light; then we will kill him.”
verses.arminianNotes: The Gazites lie in wait all night, planning to kill him at dawn. Arminian readers note that Samson's indulgence puts his life and mission at risk, showing how sin makes us vulnerable to those who seek our harm.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the enemies of God's people closing in, yet unable to act before God allows. The ambush highlights both Samson's recklessness and God's restraint of the Philistines until his own time.

verses.text: Samson lay until midnight, then arose at midnight and took hold of the doors of the gate of the city, with the two posts, and plucked them up, bar and all, and put them on his shoulders and carried them up to the top of the mountain that is before Hebron.
verses.arminianNotes: Samson carries off the city gate, posts, bar, and all, to a hill facing Hebron in Judah. Arminian readers note that his strength remains even after sin, a sobering reminder that continued gifts do not prove God's approval of conduct.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the gate, a symbol of a city's strength, is carried into Judah's heartland, a picture of Philistine power humbled. They stress that God's patience with Samson is not endorsement; judgment is coming in the next episode.
